previous.excerpt: Explore Latter-day Saint Church history through official Church History resources, the four-volume Saints history, verified topic pathways, and source-grounded questions.
previous.text: Faith, Restoration, and Remembrance Church History Meet people whose questions, choices and faith became part of the Restoration. Explore their stories through historical records, artwork and Church resources, and consider what their lives teach about discipleship. Ask a History Question Open Official Church History An illustrated Joseph Smith study The Face Behind the History Explore the death masks, portraits from life, and the creative likeness developed for focusChrist through an art-led journey. Explore Joseph’s Portrait Story The coming forth of scripture Explore Book of Mormon Evidences Follow the translation and its surviving manuscripts, compare witness accounts, and explore the record’s language and ancient context. Read the sources for yourself, then return to the book's invitation to come unto Jesus Christ. Explore the Evidences Study Read the Witness Accounts Source standard: focusChrist may summarize and explain, but the linked official Church History resources are the source of truth on this page. When a detail is uncertain or the source path does not establish it clearly, the history assistant is instructed to say so rather than fill the gap from model memory. Sacred beginnings The First Vision Begin with Joseph Smith's accounts of the experience that opened the Restoration, then follow the official historical sources as the story unfolds. Study the First Vision accounts Source-grounded study assistant Ask Church History Ask about a person, event, or question in Church history. Follow the linked Church History and Saints sources, and ask a follow-up when you want to understand more. Official Source Hub Ask about a person, event, place, practice, date, or historical question. Official Church History sources will be shown with the response. Follow-up questions stay in the same conversation until you choose New Question. AI-assisted answers are study aids and may contain errors. Unreviewed questions and limited recent context may be sent to external AI providers for research and verification. Please do not submit sensitive personal information. Faith in daily work Joseph and Emma at Harmony The history of the Restoration includes quiet days of writing, supporting, questioning, and continuing with faith. Study Emma Hale Smith A life beyond a single moment Emma Hale Smith Meet Emma across the years: a daughter in Pennsylvania, a young wife and scribe, a mother, a hymn selector and a leader among Nauvoo’s women. Follow her story through service, difficult questions, loss and the work of later life. Letters, hymns and historical accounts help us see the person within that journey. Follow Emma’s story Explore the portrait A focused priesthood study Aaronic Priesthood Follow Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery from their question about baptism to John the Baptist’s message and the baptisms that followed. Read the scriptural account alongside its historical sources, then consider how preparation, repentance, and service point toward Jesus Christ. Open the Aaronic Priesthood study A focused priesthood study Melchizedek Priesthood Study the testimony of Peter, James, and John’s ministry to Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery. Read their accounts, explore the questions that remain, and consider what the Lord teaches about serving in His name. Open the Melchizedek Priesthood study The current narrative history Read Saints Across Four Eras The Church's Saints series currently presents the history from the early Restoration through 2020 in four volumes. Use the era cards as the primary narrative path, then move into topic-specific Church History sources when a question needs closer examination. Witnesses of the record The Three Witnesses Oliver Cowdery, David Whitmer, and Martin Harris gave their names and testimony to the Book of Mormon record. Study the witnesses Volume 1 1815–1846 The Standard of Truth Early Restoration, Joseph Smith, the rise of the Church, Kirtland, Missouri, Nauvoo, and the opening of the westward exodus. Read on ChurchofJesusChrist.org → Volume 2 1846–1893 No Unhallowed Hand The pioneer era, settlement and global gathering, conflict and change, temples, plural marriage, and the closing decades of the nineteenth century. Read on ChurchofJesusChrist.org → Volume 3 1893–1955 Boldly, Nobly, and Independent A changing worldwide Church through modernization, two world wars, new institutions, growing missions, and expanding international membership. Read on ChurchofJesusChrist.org → Volume 4 1955–2020 Sounded in Every Ear The increasingly global Church, worldwide growth, temples, missionary expansion, institutional change, and the modern era through 2020. Read on ChurchofJesusChrist.org → From manuscript to book The Restoration Print Shop The translated record moved into print, where ordinary labor helped carry its witness to readers and generations beyond. Study the Book of Mormon's publication Kirtland · March 27, 1836 Kirtland: A House Built for Learning and Prayer Explore and study A house built through sacrifice People approach the temple along a worn path. Its walls recall years of shared labor and sacrifice before the dedication in 1836. Read the dedicatory prayer and consider what it means to enter the Lord’s house seeking learning, faith, and a heart prepared to serve. Read Doctrine and Covenants 109:7–9 Read Doctrine and Covenants 110 The Kirtland Temple brought worship and learning into a house built through shared sacrifice. Stone came from a nearby quarry; carpenters and other workers contributed their skills. Its assembly rooms included tiers of pulpits at opposite ends. On March 27, 1836, the Saints gathered for the dedication, and Joseph Smith offered the prayer now preserved in Doctrine and Covenants 109. Study the temple’s construction and purpose. Begin with Doctrine and Covenants 109:7–9 . The prayer brings learning, faith, order, and worship together. Let each part become a question about your own preparation. What helps you listen? What are you willing to learn? Where could greater order make room for prayer without turning your home into a place of pressure or perfectionism? Then read Doctrine and Covenants 110:1–10 , the account of Joseph and Oliver’s vision a week after the dedication. Attend to the Savior’s words and to the relationship between a sacred place and a people who seek Him. The building’s meaning reaches beyond its architecture into the lives of those who worshipped there. Consider an ordinary skill you could contribute to someone else’s spiritual growth: teaching a child, preparing a lesson, repairing something, or making a gathering welcoming. Write down one action. Remembering the temple’s builders can help us notice the quiet labor through which a community makes room for worship. Explore the Historic Kirtland Temple Practice Faithful Study Lives of faith and service Three lives, told through pictures and records Explore each life through illustrated scenes, the historical accounts, and an official Church film. John Tanner Follow John Tanner from his conversion in New York to Kirtland, Nauvoo, and the Salt Lake Valley, through journeys, generous gifts, and a remembered act of forgiveness. Read John Tanner’s story Eleazer Miller Meet the missionary whose simple witness reached Brigham Young, and follow his service from the small branches of New York to the journey west. Read Eleazer Miller’s story John Rowe Moyle Travel with the English handcart pioneer, see the work of a skilled stonecutter, and follow his return to the temple site with a handmade wooden leg. Read John Rowe Moyle’s story Kirtland's financial hopes and a painful failure Explore and study Faith amid financial loss The open ledger and Joseph’s troubled expression invite a careful look at Kirtland’s financial crisis. The losses affected real families and strained trust. Study the record honestly, then consider how humility, accountability, and compassion can guide us when hopes and decisions go wrong. Read the Kirtland Safety Society history In 1836, Joseph Smith and associates organized the Kirtland Safety Society, hoping to provide credit and support a growing community. The Ohio legislature did not grant it a bank charter. Its leaders nevertheless began operating an unchartered financial institution in January 1837. It failed that year, bringing substantial losses to Joseph and other participants. The Church's history acknowledges that disappointed expectations contributed to a crisis of confidence and faith. Read the Church's historical account . The failure had several causes. Insufficient funding, opposition, and the lack of a charter created vulnerabilities; the broader Panic of 1837 deepened the difficulties. National conditions provide context without removing responsibility for local decisions. Examine the Joseph Smith Papers' economic analysis . There were legal consequences as well: Joseph and Sidney Rigdon were tried and fined for circulating notes contrary to an Ohio banking statute. Leaders had expressed optimism about the institution, and some members felt betrayed when financial pain followed. A careful reading makes room for those losses and reactions; it does not dismiss everyone who struggled as faithless. Study the legal context and the Saints' responses . The surviving notes and financial records invite study beyond a simple success-or-failure slogan. Read Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–42 as a later standard for compassionate leadership. How can we acknowledge harm, listen to disappointment, and act with integrity? Studying difficult decisions can deepen our concern for the people affected, even when their experiences and responses differ from our own. Continue with a careful approach to historical evidence . Courage before Liberty Jail Richmond: A Voice against Cruelty Explore these moments in Church history through the pictures and the accounts linked beside them. Explore and study Courage in the room at Richmond Joseph stands before the guards while his companions remain close beside him. This scene draws on Parley Pratt’s later account of the rebuke at Richmond. Consider the courage it takes to speak with dignity when another person’s words cause harm. Read the Richmond account Read Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–44 In November 1838, before Joseph Smith was confined in Liberty Jail, he and other prisoners were held in a log house in Richmond, Missouri. Shackles and a heavy chain bound them together as they tried to rest on the cold floor. Parley P. Pratt later recalled the guards speaking boastfully about violence against the Saints. In Pratt’s account, Joseph stood and commanded them to stop in the name of Jesus Christ. The guards quieted and asked his pardon. Read the episode in Saints , chapter 31 , which cites Pratt’s later recollection and autobiography. Consider the courage it takes to defend the dignity of people who cannot answer for themselves. Then carry that question into Liberty Jail: how do conviction, compassion, and restraint belong together? The teachings that emerged there invite us to examine how we use our own words and influence. Continue into Liberty Jail Prayer, patience, and the use of power Liberty Jail: Words of Peace from a Place of Suffering In March 1839, Joseph Smith was separated from his family while the Saints struggled to find safety beyond Missouri. He and his fellow prisoners had spent months in Liberty Jail. Cold, poor food, and uncertainty wore on them. Letters could bring comfort, but they also carried news of other people’s suffering. Read the experience within the walls before turning to the words that came from them. Explore and study A prayer from within the walls Joseph’s upward gaze holds the strain of waiting and the courage to keep asking. Read his plea alongside the Lord’s answer, then bring a question of your own into prayer. Peace can begin as we turn toward Christ, even while a difficult circumstance continues. Read Doctrine and Covenants 121:1–9 Read Doctrine and Covenants 122:7–9 Bring the question into prayer “O God, where art thou?” begins the plea preserved in Doctrine and Covenants 121:1–9 . Joseph asks how long suffering will continue. The answer addresses him as a son and offers peace, endurance, and the assurance of friendship. Read the question and the answer together. Faith here includes the courage to tell God how hard the waiting has become. In Doctrine and Covenants 122:7–9 , the response turns Joseph toward the Son of Man, who descended below all things. Christ’s suffering gives the passage its depth. Consider what it means to trust His understanding while an answer, release, or healing is still beyond your sight. This is an invitation to seek His companionship in pain, never a reason to dismiss someone else’s distress. Explore and study Words for a scattered people Joseph studies pages in the quiet of the jail. His letters reached beyond those walls to people facing fear and displacement. Read the counsel about gentle influence and willing action, and consider one word of encouragement or practical kindness you could offer someone today. Read Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–46 Read Doctrine and Covenants 123:17 Let suffering change how you treat others Passages from Joseph’s March letters became Doctrine and Covenants 121 , 122 , and 123 . Explore the Church History Library’s letter exhibit. The surviving letter carries the handwriting of Alexander McRae and Caleb Baldwin, with insertions by Joseph. These were words dictated, written, and shared with a scattered Church. Examine the manuscript and its source note. The document lets us follow the counsel beyond familiar quotations into the circumstances of the people receiving it. Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–46 describes influence through persuasion, patience, gentleness, and genuine love. Read it with a relationship in mind: where could listening replace pressure? Doctrine and Covenants 123:17 joins willing action with trust in God. Choose one helpful thing within your power today, then bring what you cannot control back to Him. As you finish, write down the phrase you most need to remember. Beside it, name someone whose burden you could help carry. Let your reading become a patient conversation, a practical kindness, or a prayer offered with greater honesty. Explore Liberty Jail’s History Continue Studying Prayer Turn to Christ in Trials The Nauvoo Legion: protection, public service, and tension Explore and study Responsibility in a growing city Joseph listens as a volunteer speaks. The Legion’s history brings together the Saints’ desire for protection and the fears their growing power stirred among neighbors. Read the record with care, and consider how responsibility, restraint, and respect for others can shape a community’s peace. Read the Nauvoo Legion history The Nauvoo Legion was a contingent of the Illinois militia authorized by the city's charter, not merely an informal gathering of armed Church members. Joseph Smith became its lieutenant general on February 4, 1841. Its organization included infantry and cavalry, with regular training and public reviews. Explore the Joseph Smith Papers' records of the Legion . For people who had fled violence in Missouri, civic protection held deep meaning. Joseph described the Legion's purpose as protecting Nauvoo against mobs and enforcing the law. The Church History Museum preserves his military effects, including a cloak, epaulets, and sword, and explains the militia's place in the community. Its parades also became prominent public occasions. View the objects and their history . The same growing force that reassured many Saints alarmed some neighbors and political leaders. Questions about military power became entangled with Nauvoo's wider conflicts. In June 1844, Governor Thomas Ford ordered the Legion to surrender its state arms; the museum account records its compliance. Repeal of the city charter in January 1845 ended the Legion's legal standing under that charter. These tensions belong in the story alongside the community's desire for safety. Read about opposition and disarmament . Maudsley's historical uniform portrait helps distinguish ceremonial appearance from an imagined battle scene. Consider Doctrine and Covenants 134:1–5 : how can a community protect religious liberty while respecting the rights and security of others? Continue to faith during imprisonment or the earlier witnesses of the Book of Mormon . Nauvoo · March 17, 1842 Relief Society: Faith Organized to Care Explore and study A society ready to serve Emma meets a listener’s eyes as the women gather to organize their work. Their shared attention invites us to consider how belonging becomes service. Read the founding minutes and ask whom your own circle could strengthen through practical care. Read Mosiah 18:8–9 In the upstairs room of the Red Brick Store, women gathered to organize their service. The surviving minutes of March 17, 1842 record a meeting with prayer, discussion, decisions, and donations. Emma Smith was unanimously elected president and chose Sarah Cleveland and Elizabeth Ann Whitney as counselors. Caring for people in need was part of their stated responsibility. These pages let us hear women considering how to act together. Notice how much faithful service involves listening and deciding. The minutes preserve discussion about the society’s name and the work it would undertake. After the men withdrew, the women appointed a secretary and treasurer. Read slowly enough to notice their initiative, voices, and practical responsibilities. A record of names and motions can open into a story of people learning to share the work. Read Doctrine and Covenants 25:7–10 alongside the meeting record. Consider the relationship between learning, teaching, and encouragement. Then turn to Mosiah 18:8–10 : whose burden could you help carry without taking away their dignity or voice? Choose one need you can understand more fully this week. Ask, listen, and offer something specific. A meal, a visit, patient teaching, or shared responsibility can make care tangible. The historical record invites us to see organized service as people making room for one another, with Christ at the center of their effort. As you read, notice whose contribution you might otherwise overlook. Who keeps the record, provides the resources, notices a need, or encourages someone to speak? Give thanks for a person whose steady service has helped you belong. Explore and study Care Takes Shape in Ordinary Hands A small shirt is held up beside folded cloth as two women share the work. The early Relief Society donation record includes clothing and household textiles, reminding us how practical gifts can meet ordinary needs. Read the March 1842 donation record Explore Relief Society’s Beginnings Let Study Lead to Christ Friendship through hardship Porter Rockwell: A Friend Recognized at the Door Explore and study Recognized and welcomed Joseph’s hands rest on Porter’s arms as the two friends recognize one another. Their welcome draws us into the Christmas reunion recorded in Joseph’s journal. Think of someone returning from a hard experience: how could your attention and friendship help that person feel known? Read John 15:12–13 Explore Porter’s history and sources On Christmas Day in 1843, a road-worn stranger walked into the Smith family’s celebration in Nauvoo. His hair fell over his shoulders, and his behavior caused such a disturbance that Joseph called for him to be put outside. Then Joseph saw his face. The stranger was his old friend Porter Rockwell. Joseph’s journal records the recognition with the words “Joy untold.” After months of imprisonment and a difficult journey home, Porter had reached people who knew him. Read the contemporary journal entry. Their friendship reached back to the neighborhood where the Book of Mormon came forth. The Rockwells and Smiths were neighbors in western New York, and Porter joined the Church in 1830. He was part of the circle of friends and families whose lives became bound to the Restoration. His story opens another way to study that community alongside the scribes, witnesses, and printers who helped bring the record to readers. Explore Porter’s life. Porter’s loyalty is memorable, and his life also requires careful reading. It involved violence, accusations, and a reputation later enlarged by frontier stories. In the case behind his 1843 imprisonment, a grand jury did not indict him for the attempted murder of former governor Lilburn Boggs; that does not settle every historical question. The Church History Library explains why many familiar stories about him are difficult to verify. Examine the records behind the legends. The Christmas reunion offers something quieter to consider: what does it mean to recognize and welcome a friend after hardship? We can begin with this reunion, ask what it teaches us about friendship, and keep reading the rest of Porter’s complicated life with honesty and care. Explore the Translation Record Follow the Manuscripts into Print Read History with Care Nauvoo · 1841–1846 Nauvoo: Strength for the Journey Ahead Explore and study Hope above the river The temple rises above a city preparing for an uncertain future. Many Saints labored to finish it while also preparing to leave their homes. Study their sacrifices and the promises they carried west, then consider how worship can strengthen hope when the next step is difficult. Read Doctrine and Covenants 124:26–28 The original Nauvoo Temple rose through years of donated labor and resources. As departure from Illinois approached, Saints continued seeking its blessings. The temple was dedicated on May 1, 1846, although some portions remained unfinished. Its story holds together devotion, urgency, and loss: the building they had worked to complete could not remain their home. Read the history of the original temple. The question is personal as well as historical: what can a sacred commitment give you when your circumstances become uncertain? In her later recollection, Sarah Pea Rich described temple blessings as a source of faith for the difficult journey west. The Church’s history preserves her perspective alongside the events of construction and departure. Her memory invites us to consider strength that can be carried beyond the place where it was first received. Read Doctrine and Covenants 128:18–19 with family relationships in mind. What changes when you see your life as connected to generations before and after you? Continue with verse 22 and consider how gratitude can accompany difficult work. Choose a family story, name, or memory to preserve. Ask someone a thoughtful question and record their answer with care. You do not need a complete family history to begin honoring those who came before you. Let this study lead to a small act of remembrance, reconciliation, or service that strengthens a living relationship today. Study Doctrine and Covenants 128 Consider How Records Are Preserved History kept and studied Preserving the Record Careful preservation keeps journals, documents, photographs, and other records available for responsible historical study. Visit the Church History Library Verified official index Go Deeper by Source Type The official Church History hub brings together narrative history, topic studies, First Vision resources, women's history, historical podcasts, essays, question-based videos, and global histories. These routes are indexed into the history assistant above and remain available here for deeper study. Church History Topics Use the A–Z topic collection for people, events, practices, places, controversies, organizations, and historical developments. First Vision Study Joseph Smith's First Vision through the Church's dedicated historical resources and accounts. Women's History Explore women, organizations, experiences, and contributions across Latter-day Saint history. Joseph Smith Papers Podcasts Continue into Church-hosted historical podcast series connected with Joseph Smith-era documents and events. Gospel Topics Essays Use the Church's in-depth essays when a historical question intersects with doctrine, practice, or complex historical context. Answers to Church History Questions Follow concise Church-produced answers on frequently asked historical questions and sensitive subjects. Global Histories Study how the Church developed in countries and communities around the world rather than viewing history only through the American West. Saints Library Open all four Saints volumes together with Saints Stories and the Saints podcast from the official history library. The record endures History Preserved for Future Generations Journals, photographs and preserved records carry the faith and struggles of earlier disciples into the present. Studying them carefully helps each generation see how people sought to follow Jesus Christ. Open official Church History The center of the story Jesus Christ Across Generations Across periods, places, and people, the purpose of studying Church history is to understand the Restoration and draw closer to Jesus Christ. Explore global histories Continue the journey History, Pioneer Experience, and Open Study Pioneer Faith & History Move from the wider Church history record into the interactive pioneer journey, trail, and handcart experience. Ask Beyond History Use the broader Ask experience for scripture, doctrine, belief, personal study, or general questions. Permanent Answers Continue into indexed focusChrist answer pages with official study paths and related topics. Watch, read, and reflect See the setting, then read the record Church films can help you picture the setting. The historical sources remain the place to check details. Church video Days of Harmony Watch Oliver Cowdery’s experience as a scribe, then return to the questions and reassurance in Doctrine and Covenants 6. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Church video Sacred Grove Historic Site, Part 1: The First Vision Walk the historic setting with missionaries, then compare the surviving First Vision accounts. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Return to Oliver Cowdery and D&C 6 Work through one historical question carefully Begin with one question and give the people behind the records time to speak. For the First Vision, the Church’s First Vision Accounts essay introduces the surviving accounts and their settings. Follow its links to read the records themselves. Notice who recorded each account, when, and for whom. An event and a later recollection have different dates, and a transcript is not the original page. Read differences in context before drawing conclusions. Careful historical inquiry can sit beside prayer and reflection; each helps us ask a different kind of question. Read His words together Bring your own questions to the Savior’s words. Explore a study of reading scripture together. John 5:39 Read “Read His words together” in Jesus Christ → Place Joseph Smith in the inquiry Learn about Joseph's life and testimony, and follow the records behind the story. Explore the book and its claims Move from the historical question to what the text teaches, keeping the two inquiries clear. Carry these source habits into pioneer history Read the travelers' accounts, learn about their circumstances, and consider whom you could help today. Keep a brief note of what you learned and what remains open. The Stand Forever study can help you keep Jesus Christ in view while a historical question takes time to understand. Pause, pray, and respond Let remembrance lead to Christ Choose one invitation after reading the accounts. Give the people in the story your careful attention, then consider what the scripture asks of you today. Explore and study Friends who stay near A friend gently brushes an older woman’s hair as they talk. The Lord reminded Joseph that his friends still stood by him; ordinary acts of care can give that friendship a present-day expression. Read Doctrine and Covenants 121:9 Read Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–42 Bring an honest prayer Read Doctrine and Covenants 121:1–9 beside the Liberty Jail study. Notice the question at the beginning and the reassurance that follows. What would you like to say to Heavenly Father in your own words? You may begin with the question you actually have. Offer friendship in a hard season Return to Doctrine and Covenants 121:9 . Joseph was reminded of friends who stood by him. Think of someone whose hardship may be continuing after others have stopped asking. What welcome, practical help could you offer this week? Practice gentle influence Read Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–42 . Consider a conversation in which you want to be heard. How could patience, gentleness, and sincere love shape both your words and your willingness to listen? Choose one change you can practice. Carry a question into Ask Return to all topics

previous.pageTitle: The Mortal Ministry of Jesus Christ
previous.text: Read and discover The Son enters the water Jesus comes from Galilee to John at the Jordan. In Matthew 3:13–17 , John hesitates, recognizing that Jesus is greater than he is. Jesus asks him to proceed so that righteousness may be fulfilled. After the baptism, the Spirit descends like a dove and a heavenly voice identifies Jesus as the beloved Son. Explore and study What should we do? People bring John a practical question about how to live. His answers turn repentance toward sharing, honesty and the fair treatment of others. Luke 3:10–14 The scene joins obedience with divine witness. Father, Son and Holy Ghost are distinguishable in the account: the Son receives baptism, the Spirit descends and the Father speaks. 2 Nephi 31:5–10 reflects on why the Holy One is baptized and connects His obedience to the path He invites others to follow. His example gives baptism meaning beyond a ceremony performed in isolation from a life turned toward God. Before Luke records Jesus’s baptism, people ask John what they should do. His answers in Luke 3:10–14 concern sharing necessities, honest collection and refusing extortion. Repentance has a practical shape in the lives of those preparing to receive the Lord. Pause and consider What does Jesus’s willingness to receive baptism reveal about the way He leads? Matthew 3:13–17 2 Nephi 31:5–10 Luke 3:10–14 Read and discover An invitation becomes a friendship Come and see Andrew and another disciple follow Jesus. His invitation gives them an opportunity to spend time with Him and begin to know Him. Open study → Two of John the Baptist’s disciples follow Jesus after hearing John identify Him as the Lamb of God. In John 1:35–42 , Jesus asks what they seek and invites them to come and see where He stays. Andrew then finds his brother Simon and brings him to Jesus. The account begins with testimony but moves into personal encounter. Andrew’s part is modest and meaningful. He shares what he has found and helps another person come to the Savior. This meeting should be kept distinct from the later fishing scenes in the Gospels; John gives this encounter its own sequence and purpose. It invites us to consider how a sincere introduction, a shared passage or time spent listening may help someone explore faith without pressure. Pause and consider What do you notice about the space Jesus gives these first followers to come and see? John 1:35–42 Read and discover A question is met with an invitation Known before the meeting Philip brings Nathanael to Jesus. The conversation moves from Nathanael’s question to recognition of the Son of God. Open study → Philip tells Nathanael that they have found the One anticipated in the law and prophets. Nathanael questions whether anything good can come from Nazareth. In John 1:43–51 , Philip answers by inviting him to come and see. Jesus then addresses Nathanael personally, and the conversation opens into a testimony of His identity. The passage does not explain what happened beneath the fig tree or why Jesus’s knowledge of it mattered so much to Nathanael. We can let that detail remain open while attending to what is recorded: a question did not end the encounter. Nathanael came, listened and responded. The invitation to know Christ can include honest questions, even when the answers unfold differently from what a person first expected. Pause and consider How could Philip’s brief response help you welcome another person’s sincere question? John 1:43–51 Read and discover A need at a wedding Explore and study Fill the jars The servants attend to the stone waterpots at Jesus's direction. At Cana, their ordinary work becomes part of the first sign John records. John 2:6–9 At a wedding in Cana, Mary brings the lack of wine to Jesus’s attention. In John 2:1–11 , servants fill six stone waterpots, draw from them and take what has become wine to the person overseeing the feast. John presents this as the beginning of Jesus’s signs and connects it with His disciples’ belief. The account places His power within a shared human occasion. Mary’s instruction directs the servants toward what Jesus says, and the servants participate through concrete actions. John does not identify the bride and bridegroom or tell us their relationship to Jesus; those details need not be supplied to appreciate the scene. The sign points beyond the provision itself toward the glory of the One who gives it. Explore and study His Father’s house Jesus acts with resolve among the temple tables. John records His challenge to those who had made His Father's house a place of merchandise. John 2:13–17 John next records Jesus going to Jerusalem and clearing the temple precinct in John 2:13–17 . The sign at Cana reveals His power, while this action reveals His concern for the reverence owed to His Father’s house. Explore and study Compassion in His Father’s house Jesus turns toward a person amid the temple’s upheaval. As you read John’s account of the cleansing, consider His concern for His Father’s house and the people who came there. John 2:13–17 Pause and consider Which small actions in this account help the larger sign unfold? John 2:1–11 John 2:13–17 Read and discover A place at the table Explore and study Jesus calls Levi Jesus meets Levi at his work and calls him to follow. Levi looks toward Him, his attention turning from the counter to the invitation. Mark 2:13–15 Jesus sees Levi at the place where taxes are collected and calls him to follow. Mark 2:13–17 moves from that invitation to a meal with tax collectors, people described as sinners and Jesus’s disciples. When religious teachers question the company He keeps, Jesus answers by speaking of a physician’s work among those who need healing. Jesus's welcome and His call to repentance belong together. He draws near enough to share a meal and invites Levi into a changed life. The account asks us to look beyond the labels that can make a person easy to dismiss. Jesus sees Levi at his work and calls him toward what he can become as a disciple. Pause and consider Who might be easier to understand if you first saw a person rather than a category? Mark 2:13–17 Read and discover Women along the road Explore and study Service along the road Hands prepare provisions for the road ahead. These unnamed women picture the practical support Luke remembers from women who gave of their resources to sustain Jesus's ministry. Luke 8:1–3 Luke names Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Susanna among the women associated with Jesus’s traveling ministry. In Luke 8:1–3 , the Twelve are with Him, and women who have received healing help support the work from their own resources. The brief passage brings people into view whose service can be missed when attention stays only on the most familiar disciples. Each named woman has her own identity. Mary Magdalene is not identified here as Mary of Bethany or as the unnamed woman in another anointing account. Joanna is identified through her connection to Chuza, and Susanna is named without an extended biography. Their presence gives us enough to recognize that the ministry drew on real commitment and practical support, while leaving room for what the record does not tell us. Pause and consider Whose quiet, practical service has helped you receive something spiritually important? Luke 8:1–3 Read and discover The Twelve are sent Explore and study Sent to preach and heal The disciples begin the journey Jesus has entrusted to them. This partial gathering recalls His charge to the Twelve to proclaim the kingdom and heal. Luke 9:1–6 In Luke 9:1–6 , Jesus gives the Twelve authority and sends them to proclaim God's kingdom and heal. He asks them to travel simply and receive the hospitality offered along the way. Their service begins with His trust and with the message and authority He gives them. The disciples move from watching His ministry to participating in it. The simplicity of their preparation places attention on the commission and the households that will receive them. They leave as people entrusted with a message, not as spectators collecting another memorable experience. We can ask what we have received from the Savior that could now become useful service, and what unnecessary concerns make us slower to respond. Pause and consider Where could something you have learned from Christ become a useful act of service? Luke 9:1–6 Read and discover Hear the beloved Son Explore and study Arise, and be not afraid Jesus comes to the frightened disciples and touches them. As Peter looks up, the Savior's quiet attention accompanies His invitation to rise without fear. Matthew 17:6–8 Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain. In Matthew 17:1–9 , His appearance changes, Moses and Elias appear, and a voice from the bright cloud directs the disciples to hear the beloved Son. The disciples fall in fear; Jesus approaches, touches them and tells them to rise without fear. When they look up, they see Jesus alone. The scene brings glory and gentleness close together. The One whose face shines also reaches toward frightened followers. This happens during His mortal ministry, before His death and Resurrection, as the disciples are still learning what His mission will require. The Father’s direction to hear the Son gives them a way forward when they cannot yet understand everything they have witnessed. Listening will matter as much on the road ahead as it does on the mountain. Pause and consider What do you learn about Jesus when you see Him comfort His frightened disciples? Matthew 17:1–9 Read and discover He sees the city and weeps Explore and study He weeps over the city Jesus looks toward Jerusalem and weeps. Luke records His sorrow for a city that has not recognized the things that belong to its peace. Luke 19:41–44 As Jesus comes near Jerusalem, Luke 19:41–44 records Him looking at the city and weeping. He speaks of the peace it has not recognized and the destruction that will come upon it. The scene is distinct from His tears at Lazarus’s tomb: here His sorrow reaches toward a city and its people. His words have gravity, and His tears keep us from reading them as cold satisfaction at another’s suffering. The account invites a deeper understanding of His love, one that includes both grief and a call to recognize what leads to peace. It must never become a reason for contempt toward Jewish people. Jesus’s own life and this encounter belong within the Jewish world in which He ministered. Pause and consider What changes when you hear this warning as words spoken through tears? Luke 19:41–44 Continue with Jesus Christ Next study in the journey His miracles and compassion Stay with the people He meets and discover how particular acts of healing reveal His character. Open study → Related studies Before Bethlehem Read the divine identity that stands behind these human encounters. Open study → Miracles and Compassion Slow down with individual people who received His healing and attention. Open study → His Teachings and Parables Study the words and invitations that give direction to discipleship. Open study → The Redeemer and Risen Lord Follow the journey toward His sacrifice and Resurrection. previous.text: Read and discover The Father introduces His Son The First Vision Joseph kneels among the trees. Explore his account of the Father and the Son appearing in answer to his prayer. Open study → Joseph Smith’s published history describes his attempt to pray in the woods on a clear spring morning in 1820. In Joseph Smith—History 1:14–20 , a struggle precedes the appearance of two Personages, and one introduces the other as His beloved Son. Joseph’s question about religious belonging becomes part of a much larger encounter with God. Latter-day Saints receive this account as foundational testimony of the Father and the Son and of the opening of the Restoration. Joseph’s written witness allows us to follow the question he brought and the answer he understood himself to receive. Our own seeking may unfold very differently. Reading his account directly can encourage patient prayer and careful attention to the sources, while leaving each reader room to consider the testimony honestly. Pause and consider What question does Joseph bring, and how does the account enlarge the subject beyond that question? Joseph Smith—History 1:14–20 Read and discover Joseph and Sidney testify that He lives Explore and study We saw Him Joseph and Sidney look up from their work as the vision opens before them. Their testimony reaches beyond the room: they have seen the living Son of God. Doctrine and Covenants 76:19–24 While Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon meditate on scripture, the vision recorded in Doctrine and Covenants 76:19–24 opens their understanding. They testify of seeing the Son at the Father’s right hand and hearing the witness of His divine identity. The testimony also connects Christ with the creation of worlds and the relationship of their inhabitants to God. This is a joint witness, not a scene with Joseph alone. It contributes to the Restoration’s insistence that the risen Savior is living and active, while linking back to the scriptural witness of His creative work. The surrounding revelation explores a much larger vision of salvation. Beginning with these verses helps keep Christ Himself at the center of that study rather than treating the revelation only as a map of the life to come. Pause and consider How does this testimony connect the Savior’s present life with His identity before Bethlehem? Doctrine and Covenants 76:19–24 Read and discover The Lord accepts His house On April 3, 1836, Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery pray in the Kirtland Temple after participating in the day’s worship. Doctrine and Covenants 110:1–10 records their vision of the Lord standing upon the pulpit breastwork. He identifies Himself as the living One who was slain, speaks of forgiveness and accepts the house built to His name. The Kirtland Temple Walk toward the Kirtland Temple with its early worshippers, then explore the story of its dedication and the witnesses recorded there. Open study → The account connects divine glory with words of mercy and rejoicing. The Savior who appears with a radiant countenance speaks forgiveness and calls His people to lift their hearts. His acceptance of the temple leads toward the continuing covenant work described in the rest of the section. The building matters because of the One whose name it bears and the blessings He intends to extend through the work entrusted to His people. Pause and consider Which words in the Lord's message would you like to remember? Doctrine and Covenants 110:1–10 Read and discover The Savior’s words reach a prisoner The opening of Doctrine and Covenants 121:1–9 gives voice to Joseph Smith’s anguish while imprisoned at Liberty. His questions concern absence, suffering and the plight of the Saints. The response speaks of peace, endurance and the limits of his affliction. In Doctrine and Covenants 122:7–9 , the Savior’s descent beneath suffering becomes part of the reassurance and instruction he receives. Explore and study Listening with patience At a shared worktable, one person listens while another explains a concern. Patient attention can give practical shape to persuasion, gentleness and love. Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–44 These are words of revelation in a painful historical setting; the passages do not record a visible appearance of Christ in the cell. Nor should they be used to tell someone that every harm was divinely desired or that distress must be hidden. Joseph’s questions remain in scripture beside the answer. Their presence gives readers a way to bring anguish honestly into prayer while continuing to seek help, justice and faithful action. Later in the same revelation, D&C 121:41–44 speaks of persuasion, gentleness, kindness and love in the use of influence. Words that emerge from imprisonment can shape how a person with responsibility treats others today. Pause and consider What does it mean to you that the pleading questions were preserved together with the response? Doctrine and Covenants 121:1–9 Doctrine and Covenants 122:7–9 Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–44 Read and discover His work reaches beyond death Explore and study Messengers prepared to serve The Savior addresses the righteous spirits and sends messengers to carry the gospel onward. Doctrine and Covenants 138 places this ministry between His death and Resurrection. Doctrine and Covenants 138:18–20 Doctrine and Covenants 138:29–37 In 1918, Joseph F. Smith records a vision concerning the redemption of the dead. Doctrine and Covenants 138:11–24 describes the righteous assembled in the spirit world and Christ declaring redemption. Doctrine and Covenants 138:27–37 explains how His message reaches others: He organizes faithful messengers and commissions them to carry the gospel to those in darkness. The date of the vision and the time of the ministry it reveals are different. The passage explicitly places Christ’s described visit between His Crucifixion and Resurrection. It also says He did not personally go among the wicked. Those distinctions help us read the revelation carefully while receiving its broad hope that death does not place people beyond the reach of His redemptive work. Pause and consider How does the presence of commissioned messengers enlarge your understanding of service in Christ’s name? Doctrine and Covenants 138:11–24 Doctrine and Covenants 138:27–37 Read and discover A testimony that gathers the whole journey The Living Christ, issued on January 1, 2000, gathers the testimony of the First Presidency and Quorum of the Twelve Apostles around the Savior’s identity and mission. It connects Jehovah, creation, mortal ministry, Atonement, Resurrection, Restoration and His promised return. Its scriptural witnesses include the creative role described in John 1:1–3 and the testimony recorded in Doctrine and Covenants 76:22–24 . Explore and study A testimony sung together Voices join in a quiet room as singers follow their leader. Shared song can become an offering of faith and praise. Moroni 6:9 Doctrine and Covenants 25:12 Read the full testimony through the source link below, then return to one of the original passages it cites. That movement keeps a broad declaration connected to the scriptural accounts on which it draws. The testimony gathers the whole life and mission of Christ without limiting Him to one season or episode. It can become a useful companion as you move between the branches of this journey, remembering how each encounter belongs to the same living Savior. Testimony also finds expression in worship. Moroni 6:9 includes prayer and song in the life of the gathered Church, while D&C 25:12 gives the song of the heart a place before God. Singing can help a community attend together to the Savior it confesses. Pause and consider Which part of the testimony would you like to explore through its original scripture source? John 1:1–3 Doctrine and Covenants 76:22–24 Moroni 6:9 Doctrine and Covenants 25:12 Read and discover His love in an ordinary day Explore and study Listening before offering help At the entrance to the home, a resident explains what would help while the others listen. Useful care begins with attention to the person who will receive it. Moroni 7:45–48 Mormon’s teaching preserved in Moroni 7:45–48 describes charity through patience, kindness, humility and endurance, then connects it with the pure love of Christ. He invites hearers to pray to the Father to be filled with that love. The passage presents charity as something received and cultivated, with consequences for how a person lives. Making time, keeping a promise, bringing useful help or listening patiently to someone who is grieving can give charity a place in an ordinary day. We offer that care freely, allowing others their own feelings and response. As we pray for the pure love of Christ, we can also notice the person who needs our attention now. Pause and consider What specific act of patient love could you offer without expecting recognition or a particular response? Moroni 7:45–48 Read and discover Remembering Him together Explore and study Preparing the table Quiet preparation makes the table ready for worship. Ordinary hands attend to the bread, water and cloth before the congregation gathers. Doctrine and Covenants 20:75–79 Doctrine and Covenants 27:2 The instructions in Doctrine and Covenants 20:75–79 call the Church to meet often in remembrance of Jesus Christ and give the sacrament prayers. Their promises involve taking His name, remembering Him and keeping His commandments. The passage describes bread and wine; Doctrine and Covenants 27:2 explains that the material partaken of is not the central issue when the ordinance is received with a sincere eye to His glory. Present-day Latter-day Saint worship ordinarily uses bread and water. What the covenant remembrance asks of a disciple reaches beyond the meeting itself. Remembering Christ may change a conversation later that day, the way we repair a wrong or the attention we give a person in need. Worship and ordinary conduct belong to one life rather than two unrelated parts of the week. Pause and consider Where could your remembrance of Christ become visible in the hours after worship? Doctrine and Covenants 20:75–79 Doctrine and Covenants 27:2 Read and discover Hope while there is work to do The promise following the Ascension in Acts 1:9–11 looks toward Jesus Christ’s return. Doctrine and Covenants 45:44–52 likewise speaks of His coming in glory and connects it with resurrection, recognition and the Lord’s redemptive identity. Latter-day Saint hope reaches forward to that promised future while remaining rooted in the Savior who has already lived, died and risen. Explore and study Fear not; I am the first and the last John looks up as the risen Savior lays His hand upon him. In the vision's brightness, Christ speaks reassurance: He lives for evermore. Revelation 1:9–18 These promises do not give us authority to announce a date or label every troubling event as a settled fulfillment. They invite watchfulness that can be lived through repentance, fidelity, compassion and service. The Jesus Christ journey therefore returns to the present: the One we hope to meet is the One whose words and example can shape how we meet the people before us today. Revelation 1:9–18 offers another witness of the living Lord. John’s fear is met by the Savior’s reassuring touch and testimony of victory over death. That witness gives personal depth to the hope of meeting Him again. Pause and consider What could you do now that would be consistent with the welcome you hope to offer Him? Acts 1:9–11 Doctrine and Covenants 45:44–52 Revelation 1:9–18 Continue with Jesus Christ Next study in the journey The birth of Jesus Christ Enter the complete companion study of the promises, Nativity accounts, and witnesses of His coming. Open study → Related studies The Same Christ before Bethlehem Return to His premortal identity and the covenant witness of Jehovah. Open study → The Redeemer and Risen Lord Ground living hope in His sacrifice and the scriptural Resurrection witness. Open study → His Ministry among the Nephites Study another people’s encounter with the same living Savior. Open study → The Restored Church of Jesus Christ Continue with the existing study of Restoration claims, scripture and Church life. Open study → Sources for further study Read The Living Christ: The Testimony of the Apostles Official video: Virtual Tour of Historic Kirtland Sacrament: Topics and Questions

previous.excerpt: Explore Latter-day Saint pioneer stories, trail history, handcart journeys, sacrifice, faith, and devotion to Jesus Christ.
previous.text: Faith across the journey Pioneer Faith & History Meet the people behind the pioneer journeys. Follow their stories of faith, family, hardship and service through pictures and historical sources, and consider the choices they faced along the way. What would you like to understand? Ask about pioneer lives, journeys, and faith. Follow historical sources and related focusChrist studies beneath each answer. AI-assisted answers are study aids and may contain errors. Unreviewed questions and limited recent context may be sent to external AI providers for research and verification. Please do not submit sensitive personal information. PIONEER TOPICS The gathering begins From Nauvoo to Winter Quarters The westward story began with families leaving homes they had built, crossing the Mississippi River, and enduring the difficult first season in temporary settlements along the Missouri River. Leaving Nauvoo, 1846 Families crossed the Mississippi and began an uncertain journey west. Winter Quarters, 1846 to 1847 Temporary homes became places of preparation, worship, grief, and endurance. 1846–1847 Leaving home, preparing a way The pioneer story begins before the handcart companies. Families leaving Nauvoo crossed Iowa, endured a winter beside the Missouri and prepared for the mountains. Their road passed through Indigenous homelands, not an empty continent. Open a picture to explore its account, read the sources, or see it at full size. As you follow these journeys, listen to the people who left a record of what they experienced. February 1846 · Open picture study Crossing the Mississippi The departure from Nauvoo began with wagons ferried across the Mississippi on February 4, 1846. Families gathered at Sugar Creek in Iowa, carrying provisions and belongings into an uncertain future. When the camp moved west on March 1, the journey was only beginning: the Missouri River, not the Salt Lake Valley, would become that year’s stopping place. Leaving home is more than a line on a map. Consider what a family could carry, what it had to leave, and the help it would need from its neighbors. National Park Service: the departure Spring 1846 · Open picture study The slow miles across Iowa Rain, flooded streams and deep mud slowed the companies across Iowa. A wagon could carry a household’s necessities and still become a burden in a difficult crossing. Reaching the Missouri River took months; the hoped-for journey west unfolded through delays, illness and repeated work. Faith did not make the mud disappear. This scene invites us to notice patient effort and the ordinary hands that keep another family moving. National Park Service: the 1846 trek Garden Grove and Mount Pisgah · 1846 · Open picture study Planting for people still to come At Garden Grove and Mount Pisgah, pioneers established farms and stopping places to help later travelers. Some stayed to plant while others continued. Their service reached beyond their own immediate company: shelter and food prepared today could sustain a family arriving later. At Winter Quarters, the revelation now recorded in Doctrine and Covenants 136 joined the practical organization of travel with care for people in need. Read Doctrine and Covenants 136:8–9 and consider whose journey your preparation might lighten. National Park Service: the 1846 trek Revelations in Context: the covenant Read Revelations in Context: the covenant alongside Doctrine and Covenants 136:8–9 . The gospel purpose of a company included responsibility for those who needed help. 1846–1896 · Journey timeline · 9 milestones THE JOURNEY The Exodus Begins - February 1846 The first wagons left Nauvoo, Illinois, on February 4, 1846, beginning the westward exodus. The National Park Service estimates that nearly 70,000 Latter-day Saint emigrants followed the trail to the Great Salt Lake Valley from 1847 through 1868. Winter Quarters - 1846-1847 After crossing Iowa, the Saints established Winter Quarters on the west bank of the Missouri River in present-day Omaha, Nebraska. Other settlements and outfitting camps were established across the river in Iowa. Entering the Valley - July 21-24, 1847 Members of the advance company entered the Salt Lake Valley before Brigham Young, who was ill and traveling behind them. Young's carriage entered the camp on July 24, 1847. Pioneer Day - July 24, 1847 The arrival is celebrated. Today, Pioneer Day is a Utah state holiday commemorating this historic journey. 1850s-1900s Temple Square Development Temple Square evolves from a muddy lot to a spiritual center. The Tabernacle and other buildings transform the heart of Salt Lake City. 1853-1893 Salt Lake Temple Construction Construction of the Salt Lake Temple began in 1853. The temple was dedicated in 1893, forty years after the cornerstone ceremony. Handcart Companies - 1856-1860 About 3,000 pioneers successfully made the trek in handcart companies by 1860. The Martin and Willie handcart companies face tragic rescues in 1856. 1869 Transcontinental Railroad The golden spike was driven at Promontory Summit on May 10, 1869. The completed transcontinental railroad reduced a journey of months to days and brought the organized overland pioneer era to a close. January 4, 1896 Utah Statehood Utah became the 45th state on January 4, 1896, after a long and contested path from territory to statehood. Life between landmarks The trail was lived one day at a time Beyond the dates and destinations, the journey was made through ordinary work, long stretches beside the Platte River, and difficult crossings that required the strength of the entire company. Daily Life on the Trail Repairs, meals, animals, and family responsibilities continued with every mile. Westward Beside the Platte Companies followed the broad river corridor across the plains in natural traveling groups. Crossing the Rivers People, animals, and wagons worked together against current, rock, and cold water. A new wave of gathering · 1856 Across an ocean, then the plains The handcart story began in homes and ports far from the American plains. Preparation, limited resources and the season of departure shaped what followed. British emigration · 1856 · Open picture study The journey began across an ocean For Elizabeth Crook Panting, the plains came after an Atlantic crossing. She sailed on the Thornton with Christopher and Jane. Her brother Samuel Lane Crook was also aboard; Peter Madsen’s diary records his marriage to Sarah Haines during the voyage. Samuel and Sarah stayed in the East and did not make the Willie company’s overland journey with Elizabeth. The family also remembered a fire aboard ship: Elizabeth alerted the captain and prayed with her children. This episode comes through the family history gathered in Tell My Story, Too , rather than a ship’s log examined for this page. Tell My Story, Too: Elizabeth and Jane, pp. 101–102 Summer 1856 · Open picture study Making ready at Iowa City The Willie company journal records making tents, building carts, preparing wagons and weighing luggage. Its July entries also record births, deaths, worship and ordinary tasks such as washing clothing. Emigration was already demanding before the company began its passage across the plains on July 15. The same journal makes daily travel tangible: an early bugle, breakfast, prayers, greasing carts, packing tents and another stretch of road. These were people meeting practical needs while caring for one another. Read the Willie company journal Florence · August 1856 · Open picture study A late departure and a long road Handcarts offered a less expensive way to reach Utah, with emigrants pulling limited belongings in wooden carts. Ten companies traveled this way from 1856 through 1860. Most did not suffer the catastrophe of the late Willie and Martin companies. Their experience should not be confused with every handcart journey. At Florence, the question of continuing so late in the season was serious. The dated rescue overview below includes Levi Savage’s warning and the companies’ separate departures. Families listen together beside a waiting cart during a camp discussion. Church History: handcart companies Read the official 1856 timeline Nauvoo to the valley · Trail guide · 13 landmarks THE TRAIL These landmarks trace the route; the general route labels do not give an arrival date for every company. The Church History Pioneer Sketches exhibit documents William Clayton’s June 21, 1847 visit to Independence Rock and places the surviving drawings in the wider trail landscape. 1846 Nauvoo, Illinois The organized exodus began here in February 1846 after violence, legal conflict, and pressure against the Latter-day Saints in Illinois. Wagons crossed the Mississippi River into Iowa Territory. 1846 Garden Grove, Iowa The pioneers established Garden Grove as an Iowa way station, where they planted crops and built shelters to help companies that followed. Winter 1846 Missouri River Settlements Winter Quarters stood in present-day Omaha, Nebraska, with additional camps and settlements across the river in Iowa. This Missouri River area became the principal staging and outfitting region for westward companies. 1847 route Chimney Rock, Nebraska Famous natural landmark on the trail. This distinctive rock formation served as a beacon for weary travelers crossing the plains. Summer 1847 Fort Laramie, Wyoming This established trading post on the North Platte River was an important landmark and resupply point on several western emigrant trails. June 21, 1847 Independence Rock, Wyoming This prominent granite landmark became known for the names and dates carved or painted by travelers on the western emigrant trails. William Clayton reached it with the vanguard company on June 21, 1847. 1847 route Sweetwater River, Wyoming The trail followed and repeatedly crossed the Sweetwater River. Devil's Gate, a narrow gorge cut by the river, became one of the route's best-known landmarks. 1847 route South Pass, Wyoming Crossing the Continental Divide. This gentle pass through the Rocky Mountains opened the way to the Great Basin. July 1847 Fort Bridger, Wyoming Fort Bridger was a trading post and landmark on the final portion of the route toward the Great Salt Lake Valley. July 1847 Echo Canyon, Utah The trail passed through this narrow canyon during the final mountain approach toward the Salt Lake Valley. July 1847 Emigration Canyon, Utah Steep canyon descent into the valley. Pioneers guide their wagons through narrow passages before emerging into Salt Lake Valley. July 21-24, 1847 Salt Lake Valley, Utah Members of the advance company entered the valley before Brigham Young arrived on July 24. The company began planting crops and digging irrigation ditches soon after arrival. 1857 Mountain Meadows, Utah The 1857 Mountain Meadows Massacre occurred far south of the main 1846-1847 pioneer route. It is included here only as a separate and painful episode in territorial Utah history; follow the official Church History topic for a sourced account. A mother’s faith · The Willie company Elizabeth Crook Panting and her children A mother, a little boy and a baby stand at the heart of this account. We can honor their testimony by telling what the family preserved, identifying how it comes to us and leaving unknown details unfilled. The Willie company · 1856 · Open picture study Elizabeth, Christopher and Jane Elizabeth Crook Panting began the overland journey with Christopher, five, and Jane, one. Christopher turned six on the way west; Elizabeth turned twenty-nine in October. Their names give the migration an intimate scale: a mother, a young boy and a baby, traveling toward a hoped-for home. The Church’s historical database records all three in the Willie company. Christopher later recalled that his father, Frederick, opposed Elizabeth’s Church participation, threatened her and hid her shoes. He remembered her borrowing shoes for worship and leaving with the children; on a train, another woman exchanged clothing with her to help her avoid recognition. These details survive as his family recollection. Elizabeth in the Church History database Tell My Story, Too: Elizabeth and Jane, pp. 101–102 Elizabeth’s family account · Open picture study Fuel for a hungry camp As food dwindled on the trail, the family account remembers Elizabeth going out to gather buffalo chips for fuel. She had nearly filled her apron when an unfamiliar man approached and asked about her situation. She told him of the hunger in camp. He offered help and led her over a small hill. The remembered encounter begins with ordinary work for a family’s survival. Neither an exact date nor a securely identified cave location is supplied by the principal family account. Tell My Story, Too: Elizabeth and Jane, pp. 101–102 The account Elizabeth’s family preserved · Open picture study The gift in the cave Elizabeth followed the man to a cave where dried buffalo meat was hanging. He filled her apron with meat and instructed her to share it with others in need. After showing her the direction back to camp, he was gone. When she turned to thank him, she could no longer find either the man or the cave. The meat remained in her apron. This is the miracle as the family remembered it. The illustration leaves the stranger unidentified, as we do here. The account does not establish that he was Christ, an angel or a particular scriptural person. Tell My Story, Too: Elizabeth and Jane, pp. 101–102 Relief among the Willie company · Open picture study A gift meant to be shared Elizabeth returned and distributed the meat to people who needed food. In the family’s telling, the blessing reached beyond her own children. Jennie Edith Bell Mason’s later biography, preserved in the Church History Library, also records the cave, the dried meat and her return to the company. Her journey still required endurance. The family remembered Jane becoming dangerously ill in the handcart. Mason’s biography describes the children sheltered in a rescue wagon during the Rocky Ridge ordeal while Elizabeth walked. Mother and children reached Salt Lake City with the Willie company on November 9. Read the family biography in the Church History Library Tell My Story, Too: Elizabeth and Jane, pp. 101–102 More of Elizabeth’s story and how it was preserved The family remembered Elizabeth trusting a blessing that she and her children would reach the valley safely. Her son Wilford Woodruff Cranney later spoke of that trust and her continuing faith. The surviving compilation associates the blessing with Wilford Woodruff; its exact setting has not been independently established here. The cave account comes through later family histories, including Mason’s biography and the recollections collected by Jolene S. Allphin. Allphin cites Peter Madsen’s diary, family histories, and interviews with June Cranney Monson. A family diary is mentioned in that source chain, but its location was unknown; this page does not claim to quote an inspected original diary. Elizabeth Crook Panting is a different person from Eliza Crook. Allphin’s Eliza Crook sketch corrects an earlier misattribution of the meat account. Elizabeth’s cave must also remain distinct from Martin’s Cove and from Hanks’s later buffalo provision. Tell My Story, Too: Elizabeth and Jane, pp. 101–102 · Read the family biography in the Church History Library Read the individual records for Christopher and Jane . Faith under strain Handcarts, hardship, and rescue Most handcart companies reached the valley safely. The late departure of the Willie and Martin companies in 1856 placed them in severe autumn storms, where relief parties carried food, clothing, blankets, and hope east from Utah. The Handcart Journey, 1856 Families carried only what their carts and their own strength could bear. Rescue Wagons Arrive Relief parties met the companies with supplies, teams, shelter, and human care. October–November 1856 Go out and bring them in Willie and Martin were separate companies with different crisis points and arrival dates. Relief grew from Brigham Young’s urgent appeal into weeks of travel, giving, nursing and difficult choices. Brigham Young · October 5, 1856 · Open picture study Send help now On October 5, Brigham Young called for teams, wagons, flour and men to bring in the emigrants still on the plains. Wilford Woodruff’s journal records the concrete scale of the appeal: sixty teams, twelve tons of flour and forty additional teamsters. Concern for distant travelers became an assignment requiring immediate preparation and sacrifice. The call invites a direct question for disciples of Jesus Christ: what does another person need from me now? Read Matthew 25:35–40 beside this appeal for food, clothing and willing hands. Wilford Woodruff’s journal: October 5, 1856 Preparing the relief wagons · Open picture study The rescue began at home Women gathered bedding, clothing and other supplies while rescuers traveled east. Lucy Meserve Smith remembered the work of women in Provo to comfort those in need. Their service continued as survivors arrived; one delivery of food could not meet every need. Salt Lake City was still warm when the first appeal was made. The first relief company left on October 7, before the storm caught the emigrants on October 19. Further appeals and supplies sustained the rescue over the following weeks. Read about women’s relief efforts Church historic sites: how the rescue began Willie company · October 23, 1856 · Open picture study The hard climb at Rocky Ridge Relief did not instantly restore exhausted bodies. Daniel W. Jones later remembered rescuers bringing fuel, distributing provisions and encouraging the Willie emigrants. Some were already beyond recovery. The company still faced Rocky Ridge, a long, exposed crossing remembered for terrible suffering and loss. The dated overview records the crossing and the burials at Rock Creek. Remembering rescue also means remembering those who did not survive. Alma 7:11–12 directs our faith toward a Savior who knows suffering, rather than treating survival as a measure of anyone’s righteousness. Daniel W. Jones: later firsthand recollection Read the official 1856 timeline North Platte · October 19, 1856 · Open picture study The Martin company in the storm The Martin company crossed the North Platte as the October 19 storm struck. It would be October 28 before express riders reached them, and October 31 before supply wagons arrived. In November they sheltered in the cove near Devil’s Gate, still suffering hunger, cold and exhaustion. Jones identified Joseph A. Young, Abel Garr and himself as the riders sent to find the remaining companies. He also remembered helping pull exhausted families into camp. Later, baggage was stored at Fort Seminoe so wagons could carry people; Jones and others stayed to guard that property through winter. Read the official 1856 timeline Daniel W. Jones: later firsthand recollection With the Martin company · November 1856 · Open picture study Ephraim Hanks brings food and care In a reminiscence recorded in 1891, Ephraim Hanks described a repeated nighttime call to help the handcart travelers. When a later appeal for volunteers came, he recalled answering, “I am ready now!” He was thirty in 1856 and joined the later rescue effort; he was not one of the riders who first reached Martin on October 28. Hanks remembered praying for a buffalo, finding one, and killing another the next day. He loaded his horses with meat and brought it to hungry families. He also recalled caring for the sick and administering priesthood blessings, including a healing near Fort Bridger. His testimony includes miraculous help alongside the lasting effects of frostbite. Tell My Story, Too: Ephraim Hanks’s recollection Ephraim Hanks: life and company record 1856 at a glance: the companies and the rescue Separate companies, one sustained rescue effort Date in 1856 Event May 4 / May 25 Thornton / Horizon sail from England. July 15 / July 22–25 Willie / Martin depart Iowa City. August 13 Levi Savage advises Willie to wait until spring. August 16 / August 25 Willie / Martin leave Florence. October 4 Franklin D. Richards reports the late companies. October 5 / October 7 Brigham’s appeal / first relief company departs. October 19 Storm; riders reach Willie; Martin crosses North Platte. October 21 Supply wagons reach Willie. October 23–24 Willie crosses Rocky Ridge; thirteen buried at Rock Creek. October 27 Hanks departs with later rescuers. October 28 / October 31 Riders / supply wagons reach Martin. November 4–9 Martin shelters in the cove. November 9 Willie arrives in Salt Lake City. November 10 Hanks brings buffalo meat to Martin. November 30 Martin arrives in Salt Lake City. December 15 Final Hunt and Hodgetts arrivals. Read the official 1856 timeline More witnesses to the rescue Elizabeth Horrocks Kingsford’s later autobiography remembers her children among the hungry Martin emigrants who received Hanks’s buffalo meat. Her account offers the perspective of a family that was fed. She is a different Elizabeth from Elizabeth Crook Panting, who traveled with Willie. Elizabeth H. Kingsford’s recollection Hanks’s experiences come through a later reminiscence, not an 1856 diary. His account of providing fresh meat is separate from Elizabeth’s account of dried meat in a cave. August-October 1856 Hardships Begin The late departure left the companies on the plains as food diminished and severe autumn weather approached. Snowstorms in October intensified the crisis. Relief parties traveled east from the Salt Lake Valley and assisted the emigrants. November 4-9, 1856 Martin's Cove The Martin Company camped in the area now called Martin's Cove from November 4 to 9. The cove offered some shelter, but the emigrants continued to suffer from cold, hunger, illness, and exhaustion. November 1856 Arrival in Salt Lake The Willie Company reached Salt Lake City on November 9, and the Martin Company arrived on November 30. Residents received the survivors and helped provide food, clothing, and shelter. November 1856 The Faith and Legacy The Willie and Martin experience is remembered for suffering, rescue, faith, and the consequences of delayed departure and inadequate provisions. Read accounts of miracles and individual experiences with their sources identified, distinguishing records made during the journey from later firsthand recollections and family testimony. A destination becomes a home Arrival was the beginning of another work Entering the valley ended the overland journey, but it began years of planting, building, worship, and community life. The same faith that carried pioneers west shaped what they built after arriving. The witnesses who lived on carried both gratitude and grief into their homes and families. An elderly man recalled being a hungry boy in the Willie company. He remembered a woman sharing dried meat that she had received miraculously. Jane wept and told him that woman was her mother. Jane later told her niece, June Cranney Monson, about this encounter. For Jane, whose mother’s account had sometimes been ridiculed, his recollection was a treasured second witness. Jane had been a baby on the trek; this is her later encounter with a recipient of the food, not a claim that she witnessed the cave herself. The surviving account does not name the man or date the meeting.
